newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Fuel shortage brings agony to Nigerians.
newsitem.headline: Fuel shortage brings agony to Nigerians.

text.p: Rows of immobile vehicles, most of them battered buses and taxis, stretch as far as the eye can see at fuel stations in Lagos, commercial capital of oil producer Nigeria.
Many drivers sleep in the vehicles so they don't miss out on whatever fuel supplies are available.
The lines have become a regular part of the landscape following an acute fuel shortage that has crippled Lagos and other major towns in Africa's largest oil producing country.
"It's a shameful paradox that an oil-producing giant nation should be having fuel shortages," said Yomi Olubodun, a photo-journalist with Thisday daily newspaper.
"Government should get us out of this mess."
"Since this 'petro-agony' started, I have been trekking 30 kilometres (18 miles) daily to my office as it is difficult to get a bus or pay their fares, now triple the normal rate," said Olubodun.
"O Lord, come and save us from this season of nightmare!" moaned Anthonia Ogbe, a vegetable seller with a little girl strapped to her back and a young boy tugging at her hand.
After endless waiting at the bus-stop, she lost out in a struggle with hundreds of commuters for the only bus that arrived, already full.
"I spend a fortune on transport and buying drugs to relieve pains I get from trekking or struggling for buses," lamented street trader Abiodun Arowolo, whose business has also slumped.
The black market in fuel is booming, with those who can afford it paying as much 4,000 naira ($47) for a 50-litre (10 gallon) can of gas, more than seven times the normal price.
But for the poor like taxi driver Isiaka Kareem, getting fuel to maintain business has disrupted family life.
"Some of us don't have money to buy from the black market, so we have been sleeping daily at the pump stations," he said.

"Our wives bring our food here in the evening because we can't afford to go home to eat. Otherwise we will be too far on the line by morning," he added. Water to wash with in the morning and toothbrushes are kept in the car trunk.
Last week military ruler General Sani Abacha summoned oil ministry and state oil company NNPC officials to his Aso Rock villa in the capital Abuja to find a solution to the problem.
So far, there appears to be no solution just as there has been no definitive explanation for the cause of the shortage.
Abacha, who last September ordered a halt in fuel imports which cost the country $600 million in 1996 alone, was forced to order a resumption of the imports.
Samuel Aluko, head of an economic watchdog National Economic Intelligence Committee and NNPC sources blame the shortage on greed and corruption.

"People are benefitting from the crisis. Petroleum importers are trying to ensure that more imports are necessary and refineries are making products for export when they should be producing petrol," Aluko said.
"Importers make huge profits when they bring in ships, and by helping to engineer the crisis they make sure that imports remain necessary," Aluko said.
The bitter irony of fuel shortages in Africa's biggest oil producer has not been lost on a local press which has dubbed it a "national shame" and played up some of the fallout.
Last week they reported that a pregnant woman died, while a dozen others were severely burned in a fire at a pump station in southwestern Shagamu town during a struggle for fuel.
Nigeria, a major player in the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) produces roughly 2 million barrels per day of crude oil.
Of this, 250,000 barrels a day is allocated to four refineries that have a combined output capacity of 445,000 barrels per day of crude oil but operate well below that.
